---
title: "Modifying Lists"
unit: 2
cluster: "Working with Lists"
---

A list can be changed after it is created. This lesson covers replacing an
element, adding an element at the end, and building a new list one element at
a time.

In this lesson, we'll learn how to:

* replace an element by assigning to its index
* add an element to the end of a list with `append()`
* tell when two names refer to the same list
* build a new list with a loop and `append()`

**Assigning to an index replaces the element at that index. The `append()`
method adds an element at the end. Both change the list itself.**

## Replacing an element

This list has the names of three cities:

```{python}
cities = ["Bangalore", "Chennai", "Mysore"]
cities
```

Bangalore was renamed Bengaluru. To replace the first element, assign a new
value to index `0`:

```{python}
cities[0] = "Bengaluru"
cities
```

The assignment changed `cities`. The list still has three elements, and the
other two are unchanged.

A negative index works too. Mysore was renamed Mysuru, and it is the last
element:

```{python}
cities[-1] = "Mysuru"
cities
```

Assignment can only replace an element that exists. An index outside the list
produces an `IndexError`:

```python
cities[3] = "Delhi"
```

```text
IndexError: list assignment index out of range
```

## Adding an element

`"Delhi"` could not be added by assigning to index `3`, because that index does
not exist. The `append()` method adds an element at the end of a list:

```{python}
cities.append("Delhi")
cities
```

`append()` does not create a new list. It changes `cities` itself. The list
that had three elements now has four:

```{python}
len(cities)
```

## Two names for one list

Assigning a list to a second variable does not copy the list. Both variables
refer to the same list. This matters as soon as the list is changed.

Start with one list:

```{python}
x = [1, 2, 3, 4]
```

![`x` refers to a list.](images/names-one.svg)

Assign it to a second variable:

```{python}
y = x
```

![After `y = x`, there is still only one list. Both `x` and `y` refer to it.](images/names-shared.svg)

Now append to the list through `x`, and display `y`:

```{python}
x.append(5)
y
```

![`append()` changed the one list, so the change is visible through both names.](images/names-shared-append.svg)

The code never used `y` to change anything, but `y` shows the new element.
There is only one list, and `x` and `y` are two names for it.

**A change made through one name is visible through every name that refers to
the same list.**

### Making a copy

A slice produces a new list. Leaving out both the start and the stop, `x[:]`,
selects every element, so it makes a copy of the whole list:

```{python}
x = [1, 2, 3, 4]
y = x[:]
```

![After `y = x[:]`, there are two separate lists with the same elements.](images/names-copy.svg)

Appending to `x` now changes only the list that `x` refers to:

```{python}
x.append(5)
x
```

```{python}
y
```

![`x` refers to the changed list. `y` still refers to its own copy.](images/names-copy-append.svg)

::: {.callout-warning}
## `append()` returns `None`

`append()` changes the list. It does not return the changed list. Its return
value is `None`, Python's value for "nothing". Assigning that result to a
variable loses the list:

```{python}
numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4]
numbers = numbers.append(5)
print(numbers)
```

Call `append()` on its own line, without an assignment.
:::

## Building a new list

A new list can be built one element at a time. Start with an empty list, `[]`,
and append to it inside a loop.

This loop builds a list of the lengths of the words in a sentence:

```{python}
words = "this too shall pass".split()

lengths = []
for word in words:
    lengths.append(len(word))

lengths
```

`lengths` starts empty. Each time the loop runs, it appends the length of one
word. After the loop, `lengths` has one element for each word.

The same pattern works inside a function. This function returns a new list with
the square of each number:

```{python}
def squares(numbers):
    result = []
    for n in numbers:
        result.append(n * n)
    return result

squares([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
```

The function builds `result` and returns it. The list passed to `squares()` is
not changed.

A loop can also choose which elements to append. This function keeps only the
words longer than three letters:

```{python}
def long_words(words):
    result = []
    for word in words:
        if len(word) > 3:
            result.append(word)
    return result

long_words(["this", "too", "shall", "pass"])
```

## Summary

| Form or rule | Meaning |
|--------------|---------|
| `cities[0] = "Bengaluru"` | replaces the element at index `0` |
| `cities[-1] = "Mysuru"` | replaces the last element |
| `cities[3] = "Delhi"` with three elements | raises `IndexError: list assignment index out of range` |
| `cities.append("Delhi")` | adds an element at the end of `cities`, changing the list itself |
| `y = x` | makes `y` refer to the same list as `x`; it does not copy the list |
| a change through `x` after `y = x` | is visible through `y` too |
| `y = x[:]` | makes `y` refer to a new copy of the list |
| `append()` | changes the list and returns `None` |
| `result = []` | creates an empty list |
| a loop with `result.append(...)` | builds a new list one element at a time |

And the one idea to carry forward: assigning to an index and `append()` change
the list itself. To build a new list, start with `[]` and append to it in a
loop.
